'''Halsey Lawrence Royden, Jr.''' (September 26, 1928 – August 22, 1993) was an American mathematician, specializing in [[complex analysis]] on [[Riemann surface]]s, [[several complex variables]], and [[Differential geometry#Complex and Kähler geometry|complex differential geometry]].<ref name="StanfordNewsObit">{{cite web |url=http://news.stanford.edu/pr/93/930824Arc3164.html |title=Former dean and mathematician Halsey Royden dead at 64, Stanford News Service, 8/24/93 |publisher=news.stanford.edu |accessdate=2015-09-26 |archive-date=2022-08-20 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220820033426/https://news.stanford.edu/pr/93/930824Arc3164.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> Royden is the author of a popular textbook on [[real analysis]].<ref>{{cite book|author=Royden, H. L.|title=Real Analysis|publisher=Macmillan|year=1963}} {{cite book|title=2nd edition|year=1968}} {{cite book|title=3rd edition|year=1988}} {{cite book|title=4th edition|year=2010}}</ref>

== Education and career ==
After study at [[Phoenix College]], Royden transferred in 1946 to [[Stanford University]], where he received his bachelor's degree in 1948 and his master's degree in 1949, with a master's thesis written under the supervision of [[Donald C. Spencer|Donald Spencer]]. Royden received his Ph.D. in 1951 at [[Harvard University]] under the supervision of [[Lars Ahlfors]] with thesis ''Harmonic functions on open Riemann surfaces''.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=8310}}</ref> At Stanford University he became an assistant professor in 1951, an associate professor in 1953, and a full professor in 1958. In addition to serving on the faculty of the mathematics department, for Stanford's School of Humanities and Sciences he was in 1962–1965 associate dean, in 1968–1969 executive dean (acting dean until the vacancy was resolved), and in 1973–1981 dean. In 1981 he resigned as dean to work full-time as a mathematics professor.<ref name="MemorialRef">{{cite web|url=http://histsoc.stanford.edu/pdfmem/RoydenH.pdf|title=Memorial Resolution, Halsey L. Royden (1928–1993), Stanford Historical Society|publisher=histsoc.stanford.edu|access-date=2015-09-26|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110727070245/http://histsoc.stanford.edu/pdfmem/RoydenH.pdf|archive-date=2011-07-27}}</ref> He was on the editorial board of the [[Pacific Journal of Mathematics]] for the five years from 1956 to 1960. Royden was a visiting scholar at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in [[Princeton, New Jersey|Princeton]] for 3 months in the fall of 1969, 3 months in the spring of 1974, and for the academic year 1982–1983.<ref name="ias">{{cite web|url=https://www.ias.edu/people/cos/users/5605 |title=Royden, Halsey L. &#124; Institute for Advanced Study |publisher=ias.edu|accessdate=2015-09-29}}</ref>

In 1970, he showed the equivalence of the Kobayashi metric and the Teichmüller metric on Teichmüller space.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Royden, H. L.|title=Report on the Teichmüller Metric|journal=Proc Natl Acad Sci USA|volume=65|issue=3|date=March 1970|pages=497–499|pmc=282934|doi=10.1073/pnas.65.3.497|pmid=16591819|bibcode=1970PNAS...65..497R|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Royden was a Guggenheim Fellow for the academic year 1973–1974.<ref>{{cite news|title=Guggenheim Awards: 16 Receive Fellowships|newspaper=The Stanford Daily|volume=163|issue=38|date=17 April 1973|url=http://stanforddailyarchive.com/cgi-bin/stanford?a=d&d=stanford19730417-01.2.23&e=-------en-20--1--txt-txIN-------}}</ref> In 1974 he was an Invited Speaker (''Intrinsic metrics on Teichmüller space'') at the [[International Mathematical Congress]] in [[Vancouver]].

Upon his death he was survived by his wife (the mathematician Virginia "Jinx" Voegeli), two daughters (one, [[Leigh Royden]], a noted geologist), a son, and several grandchildren.<ref name=StanfordNewsObit/> His doctoral students include [[Alan Huckleberry]], [[Peter A. Loeb]] and [[Wetzel's problem|John Wetzel]].
